findings.title: Effect assumes browser globals
findings.explanation: This effect accesses `document` without a browser guard, so rendering or mounting in SSR, tests, or other non-DOM environments throws instead of rendering the panel.

findings.title: Duplicate metric names produce duplicate React keys
findings.explanation: The response validator allows duplicate names, but the component uses each name as a key, leading to duplicate-key reconciliation bugs and ambiguous change tracking for those metrics.

findings.title: Error responses expose arbitrary server messages
findings.explanation: The caught fetch or parsing error is rendered directly to users, which can disclose implementation details from server-provided messages; consider displaying a stable generic message and logging details separately.

findings.title: Sends the untrimmed password confirmation
findings.explanation: The request spreads all form values, so `confirmPassword` is sent to the API (and password-like data is unnecessarily duplicated); send only the fields the signup endpoint requires, typically excluding the confirmation.

findings.title: Treats error payloads as failures even on successful responses
findings.explanation: The presence of `data.errors` returns before checking `response.ok`, so a successful response containing an unrelated or stale `errors` property is displayed as a signup failure.

findings.title: Allows a successful response with an invalid ID to leave the form in an ambiguous state
findings.explanation: The account may already have been created, but the form retains the password and shows an error rather than a success state, leaving users likely to retry and potentially create duplicate accounts.

findings.title: Messages are never bounded
findings.explanation: Every distinct message remains in component state and the DOM indefinitely, so a long-lived or busy chat room can consume unbounded memory and degrade rendering performance.

findings.title: Untrusted timestamps are used as datetime values
findings.explanation: The validator accepts any string for `sentAt`, but `<time dateTime>` expects a valid machine-readable date, so malformed server data can produce misleading or invalid time metadata.

findings.title: Starts a request while the document is hidden
findings.explanation: The initial `refresh()` runs even when `document.hidden` is true, so when the page becomes visible the immediate refresh is skipped if that request is still pending, delaying fresh data until it finishes or the next polling interval.

findings.title: Does not reject duplicate metric names
findings.explanation: Duplicate names pass validation even though names are used as React keys and as the identity in `previousValues` and `changed`, causing duplicate-key warnings and ambiguous change tracking.

findings.title: User IDs may produce colliding React keys
findings.explanation: Because IDs may be strings or numbers, values such as `1` and `"1"` are coerced to the same React key, and duplicate IDs from the API also collide, which can cause incorrect list reconciliation.

findings.title: Previous results briefly remain visible for a new query
findings.explanation: Because the results are cleared in a passive effect, a render after `term` changes can still show the prior query’s results and status before the effect updates state.

findings.title: Allowed IDs can collide as React keys
findings.explanation: The `User` type permits both numeric and string IDs, so values such as `1` and `"1"` can produce the same React key and cause reconciliation errors when both appear in a result list.

findings.title: Assumes every response has a JSON body
findings.explanation: Calling `response.json()` unconditionally turns empty or non-JSON error responses (such as a 500 page or 204 response) into the generic connection-error path instead of handling the HTTP status appropriately.

findings.title: Sends the confirmation password to the API
findings.explanation: The request includes `confirmPassword`, which is only needed for client-side validation and unnecessarily transmits a second copy of the password to the server.

findings.title: Success message remains while the user edits a new form
findings.explanation: After a successful signup the form resets, but subsequent edits do not clear `accountId`, so the success message can misleadingly describe a newly edited, unsubmitted form.

findings.title: Reconnect backoff resets on every open
findings.explanation: If the server repeatedly accepts a connection and then quickly drops it, resetting `retryCount` on each `open` makes every retry use a one-second delay and can create a persistent reconnect loop.

findings.title: Messages grow without bound
findings.explanation: Every unique message is retained for the lifetime of the room session, so a long-running or high-volume chat can consume increasing memory and make rendering increasingly expensive.

findings.title: Incoming messages always force-scroll the reader
findings.explanation: Setting `scrollTop` to `scrollHeight` on every update prevents users from reading earlier messages whenever a new message arrives; only auto-scroll when the reader was already near the bottom.

findings.title: Storage-backed state can break server hydration
findings.explanation: When rendered on the server, `readTodos` falls back to an empty list, while the browser initializer may load saved todos, producing different server and client markup; the subsequent persistence effect can then overwrite the saved list with the client’s initial state.

findings.title: Local-storage initialization can cause hydration mismatches
findings.explanation: When rendered on the server, this initializer returns an empty list because `window` is unavailable, but the client may initialize from saved todos, so the server and first client renders differ during hydration.

findings.title: Adding a task can throw when `crypto.randomUUID` is unavailable
findings.explanation: In browsers or contexts without `crypto.randomUUID` (including some insecure contexts), submitting a task throws instead of adding it, so provide a supported ID-generation fallback or handle the failure.

findings.title: Elapsed time may stop advancing during device sleep
findings.explanation: `systemUptime` measures awake time on Apple platforms, so locking the device or otherwise sleeping can make the stopwatch undercount elapsed time; use a monotonic clock that includes sleep if the stopwatch should continue through it.

findings.title: Disappearing the view stops the stopwatch
findings.explanation: `onDisappear` also runs for temporary navigation, tab, or presentation changes, so leaving the screen unexpectedly stops timing instead of allowing the stopwatch to continue.

findings.title: UserDefaults observer reloads for unrelated suites
findings.explanation: `UserDefaults.didChangeNotification` is observed globally, but the handler never checks which defaults instance or suite changed, so unrelated preference writes can trigger redundant reloads and interfere with this store's state.

findings.title: External writes can be overwritten during reload
findings.explanation: The defaults notification schedules an asynchronous main-actor reload, leaving a window where a user edit can write an older value back to `UserDefaults` before the external change is loaded.

findings.title: Invalid persisted refresh intervals reach the Stepper
findings.explanation: Values loaded from `UserDefaults` are not validated or clamped to the Stepper's 60–3,600 second range, so stale, negative, infinite, or out-of-range stored values can make the control show invalid state and persist unusable intervals.

findings.title: Refresh interval persistence compares floating-point values exactly
findings.explanation: Exact `Double` inequality can cause needless writes for numerically equivalent interval values, so consider representing this minute-based setting as an integer or comparing normalized values.

findings.title: Decode results off the main actor
findings.explanation: `search(for:)` is main-actor isolated, so decoding a large response runs synchronously on the UI thread and can cause visible hangs; move decoding to a non-main-actor context.

findings.title: Ensure result IDs are unique
findings.explanation: `List` uses each result's `id` as its row identity, so duplicate IDs in the API response can produce incorrect row updates or SwiftUI identity warnings.

findings.title: Observe changes from the injected defaults suite
findings.explanation: This publisher uses the process-wide `UserDefaults.didChangeNotification`, which is posted for changes to the standard defaults rather than reliably identifying changes to the injected `defaults` instance, so stores backed by a custom suite can miss external updates.

findings.title: Queued reloads can overwrite newer local edits
findings.explanation: Each defaults notification schedules an uncoalesced main-actor task, so a delayed reload can read and apply stale defaults after the user has made a newer in-memory edit.

findings.title: Out-of-range stored refresh intervals break the Stepper
findings.explanation: The persisted `Double` is accepted without validation, so a value outside `1...3600` can put the bound Stepper outside its supported range and leave the UI displaying or editing an invalid interval.

findings.title: Decode results off the main actor
findings.explanation: `SearchViewModel` is main-actor isolated, so decoding the response array runs on the UI actor and can block rendering for a large payload; perform decoding in a nonisolated/background context.

findings.title: Cancellation can leave loading state set
findings.explanation: When the view’s `.task` is cancelled without a replacement search (for example, when the view disappears), this early return skips resetting `isLoading`, so the retained view model can remain stuck in its loading state.

findings.title: Creates an unstructured task for every timer tick
findings.explanation: At 100 ticks per second, each fire enqueues a MainActor task that cannot be cancelled, so if the actor is busy these tasks can accumulate and later perform redundant updates.

findings.title: Unbounded image downloads can exhaust memory
findings.explanation: `data(from:)` buffers the entire response without a size limit, so a large or malicious response can consume substantial memory before decoding or caching it.

findings.title: Full-size image decoding runs on the main actor
findings.explanation: The cache and its download task are main-actor isolated, so constructing `NSImage` from downloaded data can block UI updates, especially for large images.

findings.title: Cache limit does not bound image memory usage
findings.explanation: `countLimit` caps the number of cached objects rather than their memory cost, and caching full-resolution images can still retain a large amount of memory.

findings.title: Backoff is not reset when a connection succeeds
findings.explanation: `retryDelay` resets only after receiving a frame, so a connection that repeatedly completes its handshake but drops before the first message can keep escalating to the 30-second delay despite each successful connection.

findings.title: Unbounded inbound messages can exhaust memory
findings.explanation: Every decoded server message is retained indefinitely, and neither individual payload size nor the message history is bounded, allowing a busy or hostile server to grow memory usage without limit.

findings.title: Cache retains every decoded image indefinitely
findings.explanation: The shared cache has no eviction or size limit, so scrolling through many distinct URLs keeps all decoded `NSImage` instances alive and can cause substantial memory growth.

findings.title: Downloads have no response-size limit or downsampling
findings.explanation: The code buffers the entire response and decodes it at full resolution, allowing unexpectedly large images or responses to consume excessive memory before they are displayed as small thumbnails.

findings.title: Progress stream uses unbounded buffering
findings.explanation: `AsyncStream` defaults to an unbounded buffer, so a fast or long-running SDK can accumulate progress events indefinitely when the consumer is slower, causing unnecessary memory growth; consider a bounded or newest-value buffering policy.

findings.title: User IDs can collide as React keys
findings.explanation: The validator accepts both numeric and string IDs, but React coerces keys to strings, so distinct users with IDs `1` and `"1"` (or duplicate IDs) can share a key and be reconciled incorrectly.

findings.title: User IDs may produce colliding React keys
findings.explanation: The response validator permits duplicate IDs and both numeric and string IDs, which can stringify to the same React key (for example, `1` and `"1"`), causing incorrect row reconciliation and React warnings.

findings.title: Duplicate metric names are accepted
findings.explanation: The validator allows repeated names, which produces duplicate React keys and makes the name-keyed change tracking ambiguous or incorrect.

findings.title: Auto-scroll overrides the reader’s scroll position
findings.explanation: Every content-height preference change scrolls to the bottom, so incoming messages or layout changes pull users away from older messages even when they have intentionally scrolled up.

findings.title: WebSocket URL points to a placeholder host
findings.explanation: `chat.example.com` is a reserved example domain, so the connection cannot reach a real chat service unless this value is replaced with the configured endpoint.

findings.title: Connection status can remain stale after send failure
findings.explanation: This branch marks the connection disconnected but leaves `status` as “Connected” until the receive loop observes cancellation and updates it.

findings.title: Treat non-2xx responses before parsing errors
findings.explanation: The code parses JSON before checking `response.ok`, so an error response with an empty or non-JSON body throws and is reported as an ambiguous connection failure instead of the intended request failure.

findings.title: Handle malformed or empty JSON responses
findings.explanation: Calling `response.json()` unconditionally rejects for successful responses with empty or invalid JSON, leaving the user with an uncertain-creation message even when the server response should be handled as a protocol error.

findings.title: Do not discard unrecognized server validation errors
findings.explanation: If the server returns a nonempty `errors` object containing only unknown fields or non-string messages, the form ignores those details and reports a generic error without displaying actionable feedback.

findings.title: Avoid rendering an untrusted account ID as text
findings.explanation: The ID is interpolated without trimming a string value, so a valid but whitespace-padded server ID is shown verbatim and may create confusing success feedback.

findings.title: Metric names are not guaranteed to be unique keys
findings.explanation: If the API returns multiple metrics with the same name, React receives duplicate keys and the name-based change tracking becomes ambiguous, so validate uniqueness or use a stable unique identifier.

findings.title: Invalid content inside the description list
findings.explanation: The `dl` grouping `div` contains a `span` in addition to its `dt`/`dd` pair, which is not valid description-list grouping markup and can confuse assistive technology.

findings.title: Message history grows without bound
findings.explanation: Every unique message remains in component state and the DOM for the lifetime of the room, so a long-lived or busy chat can consume unbounded memory and degrade rendering performance.

findings.title: Guard queued messages against room changes
findings.explanation: A message update queued just before the room effect is cleaned up can run after the new room has been selected and append an old-room message to the new room's state, so the updater should verify `current.id === roomId` before adding it.

findings.title: Local-storage initialization can cause an SSR hydration mismatch
findings.explanation: When rendered on the server, `restoreTodos()` returns an empty list, while the browser may initialize from saved todos, so the initial client markup can differ from the server markup and trigger hydration errors.

findings.title: Server rendering can hydrate with different todos
findings.explanation: The lazy initializer reads browser storage during render, so an SSR render starts with an empty list while the client may render stored todos immediately, causing a hydration mismatch and potentially replacing server-rendered content.

findings.title: Malformed stored data is overwritten on mount
findings.explanation: When parsing fails, the loader returns an empty list and the mount effect then persists that empty list, discarding the original stored value rather than preserving it or surfacing a load error.

findings.title: Todo creation assumes randomUUID is available
findings.explanation: Calling `crypto.randomUUID()` directly can throw in browsers or contexts that do not support it, preventing the add action from completing.

findings.title: Search uses a placeholder API host
findings.explanation: Requests are sent to `api.example.com`, so this screen cannot retrieve real search results unless the placeholder is replaced with the intended service endpoint.

findings.title: Serialization can throw or collapse distinct inputs
findings.explanation: `JSON.stringify(ids)` can throw for malformed runtime inputs such as circular arrays and may yield `undefined` for unsupported values, which can break the effect's `JSON.parse` or cause distinct ID lists to share a request key.

findings.title: Resetting the editor on server updates can discard drafts
findings.explanation: Including `displayName` and `bio` in the React key remounts the form whenever those props change, so a background refresh can silently erase a user's unsaved edits.

findings.title: Successful save can mark a stale draft as saved
findings.explanation: The submit handler closes over the submitted `draft` and calls `setSaved(draft)` after awaiting `onSave`; if the draft changes while the request is in flight, the newer edits are incorrectly treated as saved and the dirty indicator is lost.

findings.title: Disappearing view silently pauses the stopwatch
findings.explanation: Calling `stop()` on every disappearance changes stopwatch state when the view is merely covered or temporarily removed, so returning to the stopwatch does not resume elapsed time despite the view documenting pause/resume controls.

findings.title: Lap identifiers can be reused after clearing laps
findings.explanation: Using the current array count for IDs means removing laps through `reset()` causes later laps to reuse identifiers, which can confuse SwiftUI identity if updates overlap or the model is extended to preserve displayed rows.

findings.title: Decode search results off the main actor
findings.explanation: `search(for:)` is main-actor isolated, so decoding the response here runs synchronously on the UI thread and can make the interface unresponsive if the response is large.

findings.title: Truncation can display hundredths incorrectly
findings.explanation: Converting the binary floating-point product directly to `Int` truncates values, so an elapsed time intended to show a hundredth such as `0.29` can display one hundredth too low; round before converting.

findings.title: Timer publishes more often than the display can use
findings.explanation: A 10 ms timer drives SwiftUI updates at 100 Hz even though the UI displays hundredths and most screens refresh less frequently, causing avoidable main-thread and battery work.

findings.title: Validate persisted refresh intervals
findings.explanation: The stored interval is accepted without checking the Stepper’s 15...3,600 range, so an out-of-range value can be loaded and displayed even though the control is supposed to constrain it.

findings.title: Validate persisted refresh intervals
findings.explanation: The stored integer is loaded without checking the Stepper’s `1...1_440` range, so stale or malformed preferences can leave the setting outside the range the UI promises.

findings.title: Decode images off the main actor
findings.explanation: The task is explicitly main-actor-isolated, so constructing and validating an `NSImage` happens on the UI actor and can cause visible hangs for large or complex images.

findings.title: Bound downloaded image data and dimensions
findings.explanation: The code buffers the entire response and accepts arbitrarily large image dimensions, so a URL serving oversized content can cause excessive memory use or a process termination.

findings.title: Use a memory-cost limit for the image cache
findings.explanation: `countLimit = 200` limits only the number of entries, not their memory cost, so caching 200 full-resolution images can still consume an unbounded amount of memory.

findings.title: Duplicate URLs receive duplicate view identities
findings.explanation: The outer `ForEach` uses unique indices, but `.id(imageURLs[index])` overrides that identity with the URL, so repeated URLs have duplicate identities and SwiftUI may reuse or reconcile their cell state and tasks incorrectly.

findings.title: Image decoding runs on the main actor
findings.explanation: `ThumbnailCache` and its download task are main-actor isolated, so constructing `NSImage` from downloaded data happens on the UI actor and can stall scrolling when images are large or numerous.

findings.title: Geocoding cancellation can remain suspended indefinitely
findings.explanation: Cancellation is only checked after the callback resumes the continuation, so a canceled task still waits forever if the geocoder never calls back; use a cancellation-aware bridge if callers need prompt cancellation.

findings.title: Geocoding cancellation cannot unblock the task
findings.explanation: If the task is cancelled while the legacy geocoder is pending, it remains suspended until the callback arrives, so the cancellation check after the continuation does not provide prompt cancellation.

findings.title: Upload cancellation still waits for completion
findings.explanation: Cancelling the task while it awaits the continuation does not make `upload(file:)` return until the SDK invokes `onFinish`, leaving callers and any structured-concurrency scope blocked despite cancellation.

findings.title: Progress stream uses unbounded buffering
findings.explanation: `makeStream()` defaults to unbounded buffering, so a fast or unusually chatty SDK can accumulate progress events without limit when the consumer is slower.

findings.title: Reconnect backoff resets on any received message
findings.explanation: A connection that repeatedly delivers one message and then drops resets `retryDelay` to one second each time, allowing a flapping server to trigger rapid reconnects instead of backing off.

findings.title: Received messages accumulate without a bound
findings.explanation: The WebSocket stream appends every incoming message indefinitely, so a long-lived or high-volume chat session can grow memory usage without limit.
